name: Direct curl to sh execution
description: Detects pattern where content is downloaded via curl and piped directly into a shell execution context, a common malware delivery technique.
falsePositiveGuidance: Legitimate setup scripts sometimes use this pattern, though it is discouraged in production AI skills.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1059.004

name: Child Process Execution
description: Identifies the usage of child_process.exec which allows arbitrary shell command execution with the privileges of the Node process.
falsePositiveGuidance: May trigger on administrative scripts running valid system commands.
references: CWE-78: OS Command Injection

name: Spawn Process
description: Identifies the usage of child_process.spawn. While safer than exec, it can still be used to launch malicious binaries.
falsePositiveGuidance: Common in tools that orchestrate other CLI utilities.
references: OWASP Top 10: A03:2021-Injection

name: Base64 Decoded Execution
description: Detects execution of base64 decoded strings, highly indicative of obfuscated payloads.
falsePositiveGuidance: Rarely a false positive. Obfuscated commands are inherently suspicious.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1027 - Obfuscated Files or Information

name: Wget to sh
description: Detects download via wget piped to shell execution.
falsePositiveGuidance: Similar to curl | sh, used by some legitimate installers.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1105 - Ingress Tool Transfer

name: Python one-liner shell
description: Detects usage of python -c to spawn a reverse shell or execute arbitrary code.
falsePositiveGuidance: Security scanning tools might legitimately contain these signatures.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1059.006 - Python

name: Read Sensitive System Files
description: Detects attempts to read sensitive Linux/Unix system files like /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow which can lead to privilege escalation.
falsePositiveGuidance: System auditing tools will naturally read these files.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1003.008 - /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow

name: SSH Key Exfiltration
description: Detects direct access to ~/.ssh/id_rsa or similar private key files.
falsePositiveGuidance: Tools designed for SSH key management will trigger this.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1552.004 - Private Keys

name: Write to Startup Scripts
description: Detects modification of shell profile scripts to establish persistence.
falsePositiveGuidance: Legitimate developer tool installers (like nvm or rustup) modify these profiles.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1546.004 - Unix Shell Configuration Modification

name: Dangerous File Deletion
description: Detects indiscriminate deletion commands like rm -rf / or rm -rf /*.
falsePositiveGuidance: Almost never legitimate unless operating inside an isolated ephemeral container script.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1485 - Data Destruction

name: Node.js FS Unlink
description: Detects programmatic deletion of files using Node.js fs.unlink or unlinkSync.
falsePositiveGuidance: Very common in scripts that clean up temporary files.
references: CWE-73: External Control of File Name or Path

name: Hidden Directory Creation
description: Detects creation of hidden directories (starting with .) which is often used to hide malware payloads.
falsePositiveGuidance: Many standard tools create hidden configuration directories (e.g. .git, .npm).
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1564.001 - Hidden Files and Directories

name: Data to Pastebin
description: Detects HTTP requests directed to pastebin.com or similar clipboard sharing sites, often used for data exfiltration.
falsePositiveGuidance: Sometimes used legitimately to download configuration snippets or share crash logs.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1567.002 - Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

name: Discord Webhook Exfiltration
description: Detects hardcoded Discord webhook URLs which are frequently abused as C2 or exfiltration channels.
falsePositiveGuidance: Valid usage exists in notification scripts or bots.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1567 - Exfiltration Over Web Service

name: Dynamic Fetch URL
description: Detects fetch or HTTP requests where the URL is dynamically constructed, hiding the destination.
falsePositiveGuidance: Extremely common in API wrapper libraries.
references: CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

name: DNS Exfiltration
description: Detects patterns of embedding sensitive data in DNS lookup requests (e.g. via ping or dig to custom subdomains).
falsePositiveGuidance: Used extensively by penetration testers and bug bounty scanners.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1048.003 - Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Unencrypted/Obfuscated Non-C2 Protocol

name: IP Address Hardcoding
description: Detects hardcoded raw IP addresses instead of hostnames, typical in rudimentary C2 beacons.
falsePositiveGuidance: Local IP addresses (127.0.0.1, 192.168.x.x) are widely used in development.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1008 - Fallback Channels

name: Netcat Reverse Shell
description: Detects usage of netcat (nc) to pipe shell input/output over a network socket.
falsePositiveGuidance: Rarely a false positive. Direct reverse shell execution is highly suspicious.
references: MITRE ATT&CK: T1059 - Command and Scripting Interpreter

name: Ignore Previous Instructions
description: Detects explicit attempts to override the system prompt and reset the LLM context.
falsePositiveGuidance: May trigger in meta-prompts or AI debugging contexts.
references: OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection

name: Role Assumption (DAN)
description: Detects jailbreak patterns like Do Anything Now (DAN) or forced persona adoption.
falsePositiveGuidance: Legitimate role-playing prompts (e.g. "Act as a senior developer") can sometimes overlap.
references: OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection

name: System Prompt Leakage
description: Detects requests asking the AI to print its initial instructions or system prompt.
falsePositiveGuidance: Usually malicious, though prompt engineers might test this.
references: OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection

name: Payload Encoding Injection
description: Detects base64 or hex encoded payloads in the prompt designed to evade simple keyword filters.
falsePositiveGuidance: Users providing encoded data for legitimate processing tasks (e.g. decode this string).
references: OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection - Obfuscation

name: Urgency Manipulation
description: Detects manipulative urgency tactics to bypass safety checks (e.g. "This is a life or death emergency").
falsePositiveGuidance: Users might genuinely write urgent prompts, though context is key.
references: Social Engineering: Urgency Techniques

name: Deceptive Safe Assertion
description: Detects prompts asserting that their requested action is completely safe or authorized by administrators.
falsePositiveGuidance: Can be conversational filler.
references: Social Engineering: Authority/Trust Techniques

name: Eval Execution
description: Detects the use of JavaScript eval() which executes arbitrary string expressions as code.
falsePositiveGuidance: Some legacy codebases or dynamic templating engines use eval, but it is highly discouraged.
references: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

name: Function Constructor Execution
description: Detects the use of the Function constructor to generate anonymous functions from strings, an eval alternative.
falsePositiveGuidance: Used in some high-performance templating libraries (e.g. doT.js).
references: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code

name: Dynamic Import
description: Detects usage of dynamic import() with non-literal arguments, which can load arbitrary modules.
falsePositiveGuidance: Common in modern applications with dynamic chunk loading or plugins.
references: CWE-470: Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code ('Unsafe Reflection')

name: SetTimeout Code Execution
description: Detects setTimeout or setInterval called with a string argument instead of a function, which acts like eval.
falsePositiveGuidance: Legacy code pattern, rarely seen in modern codebases.
references: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code

name: Process Env Access
description: Detects access to process.env, which may be used to exfiltrate secrets or manipulate environment context.
falsePositiveGuidance: Extremely common for reading configuration variables.
references: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

name: Python Exec/Eval
description: Detects the use of Python exec() or eval() on strings, allowing arbitrary code execution.
falsePositiveGuidance: Very rare in secure codebases, highly suspicious.
references: CWE-95: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code ('Eval Injection')
